Abstract
The current healthcare system struggles to respond quickly enough to provide emergency medical care, 
particularly in remote or densely populated areas, or cannot scale to adequate levels of response in real-time. This 
paper presents an elaborate adaptive edge-fog healthcare network framework that supports Electronic Medical 
Records (EMR) through a multi-layer optimised solution. It also includes a real-time, decentralised processing model 
based on edge and fog computing architectures, which avoids the high latency typically required by most cloud-
based systems when processing important data closer to its origin. To achieve this end, several novel features 
have been proposed within this framework, including a dynamic resource allocation algorithm that balances 
the computational load on the target edge and/or fog nodes as necessary to achieve optimal performance and 
prevent system failure. Furthermore, the operational environment of the framework incorporates robust and reliable 
methods for fault tolerance and data protection against leakage, even in low-connectivity networks or with node 
loss. Large-scale experiments demonstrate that the framework achieves a latency reduction rate of 66.67%, an 
energy consumption improvement of 92%, and a reliability of 96% in failure cases, thereby outcompeting cloud-
only architectures in disaster recovery scenarios. Interestingly, the findings presented can demonstrate how the 
framework’s utilization may revolutionise healthcare emergency management by offering fast, safe, and efficient 
data-supported assistance in various care contexts.

Introduction
The growing frequency of natural disasters, pandem­
ics, and large-scale accidents has placed immense pres­
sure on healthcare organizations worldwide. The World 
Health Organization (WHO) estimates that nearly 
265 million people require emergency medical care annu­
ally due to natural disasters alone [1]. Timely response in 
such scenarios is critical, as delays in medical interven­
tion can significantly impact patient survival rates [2–4]. 
However, existing healthcare infrastructures often fail to 
provide real-time data processing and decision-making 
capabilities, particularly in remote or congested urban 
environments [5–9].
Traditional cloud-based healthcare networks, which 
rely on centralized data centres for processing and stor­
age, have severe limitations in emergencies. These sys­
tems introduce high latency, suffer from bandwidth 
congestion, and depend on stable connectivity to distant 
servers, making them unsuitable for real-time emergency 
response [10, 11]. In life-threatening medical emergen­
cies, where every millisecond counts, delays in process­
ing vital patient data—such as cardiac signals or oxygen 
saturation levels—can be fatal. The limitations of central­
ised cloud computing in emergency healthcare have led 
to the adoption of decentralised computing paradigms, 
such as edge and fog computing. Edge computing allows 
real-time data processing closer to the source (e.g., IoT-
enabled medical devices), while fog computing acts as an 
intermediary, aggregating and processing data between 
the edge and the cloud. This distributed approach sig­
nificantly reduces latency, improves bandwidth efficiency, 
and ensures fault tolerance [5, 10]. However, despite 
these advantages, current edge-fog healthcare models 
still struggle with several critical challenges. Emergency 
response networks must balance computational loads 
across edge and fog nodes, ensuring that no single node 
is overloaded while maintaining low latency [12]. Health­
care systems must remain operational even in the face of 
node failures, low connectivity, or network congestion, 
ensuring uninterrupted service during crises [13]. Sensi­
tive patient information must be protected from unau­
thorized access while maintaining real-time availability 
[3, 14]. During mass casualty incidents (e.g., pandemics 
and earthquakes), networks experience an overwhelm­
ing influx of data, requiring efficient load balancing and 
adaptive processing strategies [15, 16].
Real-world case study – adaptive edge-fog emergency 
response in smart hospitals
To demonstrate the real-world applicability of the 
proposed Adaptive Edge-Fog Healthcare Network 
(AEFM), we consider an emergency response scenario 
in a large-scale urban smart hospital equipped with IoT-
enabled patient monitoring systems. Wearable devices 
continuously track vital signs including heart rate, blood 
pressure, and SpO₂, ensuring 24/7 visibility of patient sta­
tus across emergency and ICU wards.
In one critical event, a patient’s heart rate rapidly 
spiked beyond 120 bpm, which was immediately detected 
by the edge device using onboard anomaly detection. 
Instead of offloading this raw data to distant cloud serv­
ers, the alert was transmitted to a fog node positioned 
within the hospital network. The fog node aggregated 
additional sensor inputs (e.g., oxygen levels, BP trends) 
and executed an AI-powered predictive model to assess 
the risk of cardiac arrest.
Upon confirming high-risk status, the fog node gener­
ated an emergency alert, directly notifying the attend­
ing ER physicians and triggering hospital-side dispatch. 
The system dynamically Balanced the load by assigning 
the task to Fog Node 1. In case of resource overload, it 
rerouted the task to Fog Node 2 without human interven­
tion. Meanwhile, non-urgent patient data was securely 
sent to the cloud for longitudinal health analysis.
This edge-fog-localized response pipeline reduced end-
to-end decision latency from 1500 ms (in cloud-only sys­
tems) to under 500 ms. The case validates how AEFM 
enables real-time responsiveness, ensures fault toler­
ance via automated failover and load balancing, and con­
serves energy by minimizing long-range data transfers. 
Moreover, the integration of AI at the fog layer improved 
patient triage precision and contributed to long-term 
model retraining through secure cloud synchronization.
A comprehensive performance evaluation of this sce­
nario is presented in Sect.  5.3, highlighting improve­
ments in latency, throughput, fault tolerance, and 
reliability compared to traditional cloud-based and edge-
only models.
To address these challenges, this research proposes a 
novel Adaptive Edge-Fog Healthcare Network Frame­
work for real-time emergency response management. 
This framework is designed to dynamically allocate com­
puting resources, enhance fault tolerance, and ensure the 
secure and low-latency processing of medical data in crit­
ical healthcare situations. This paper presents a compre­
hensive edge-fog healthcare framework that integrates 
intelligent resource management, decentralised comput­
ing, and adaptive fault-tolerant mechanisms to enhance 
emergency medical response capabilities. The key contri­
butions of this research are:
a)	 A novel edge-fog healthcare network architecture 
that minimizes latency by optimally processing 
critical patient data at the edge while offloading non-
urgent tasks to fog and cloud layers.
b)	A dynamic resource allocation strategy that balances 
computational workloads across edge and fog nodes

Research motivation
Although edge and fog computing offer promising solu­
tions for reducing latency and improving reliability in 
emergency healthcare systems, they lack cohesive frame­
works that combine AI-driven caching, predictive work­
load allocation, and cold start latency mitigation in a 
unified architecture. Existing solutions fail to support 
real-time emergency interventions at scale, especially 
during disasters or mass casualty events. To bridge these 
gaps, we propose a comprehensive, adaptive edge-fog 
model designed for dynamic, secure, and low-latency 
emergency response management.

Literature review
The integration of edge and fog computing in healthcare 
emergency response has been extensively explored in 
recent literature. Many studies have focused on reducing 
latency, improving fault tolerance, enhancing security, 
and optimizing dynamic resource allocation in health­
care networks. However, most existing approaches face 
significant scalability and adaptability challenges in real-
world emergency scenarios.
Existing work on edge-fog computing in healthcare 
networks
Several studies have explored edge-fog architectures to 
overcome the limitations of cloud-based systems. For 
example, Agnihotri et al. [2] reviewed the applications of 
fog computing in healthcare, highlighting its capabilities 
for reducing latency. However, their study highlighted 
security concerns and the lack of standard regulatory 
frameworks. Similarly, Alam et al. [3] introduced a block­
chain-based fog computing system for IoMT applica­
tions, which improved data integrity and reliability but 
incurred high computational overhead, making it less 
suitable for real-time emergency cases.
Kamruzzaman et al. [12] proposed a blockchain-
enabled fog system for secure healthcare data exchange, 
showing improvements in transaction response time. 
However, the framework exhibited scalability limita­
tions when handling large data streams in high-density 
healthcare settings. On the other hand, Sachin et al. [19] 
designed FedCure, a Federated Learning (FL)-based solu­
tion for intelligent healthcare. While FL improved per­
sonalization in patient monitoring, it introduced data 
heterogeneity issues, making real-time decision-making 
difficult.
More recent studies have focused on AI-driven opti­
mization strategies. Liu et al. [17] implemented Deep 
Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for dynamic resource 
allocation in edge-fog healthcare systems, achieving 
improved latency and energy efficiency. However, their 
model struggled with scalability under high workloads. 
Similarly, Monti et al. [20] proposed a transfer learning-
based approach to medical data analytics, which pro­
vided higher accuracy but introduced privacy risks due to 
data sharing between edge and fog nodes.
Edge-fog computing has emerged as a pivotal architec­
ture to overcome the limitations of traditional cloud-cen­
tric systems in healthcare, particularly in emergency and 
time-critical scenarios. Numerous studies have investi­
gated various mechanisms to improve latency, reliability, 
and energy efficiency in healthcare Internet of Things 
(H-IoT) environments.
Aghazadeh et al. [21] presented an in-depth review of 
proactive content caching mechanisms in edge environ­
ments, highlighting their applicability to healthcare by 
minimising content retrieval delays and enhancing user 
quality of service (QoS). Jazayeri et al. [22] proposed a 
latency-aware and energy-efficient offloading scheme 
based on Hidden Markov Models (HMM), demon­
strating significant gains in mobile fog environments, 
although with limitations in adaptive resource realloca­
tion under dynamic load spikes.
Mustafa et al. [23] employed Deep Reinforcement 
Learning (DRL) with Duelling DQN to perform par­
tial task offloading in Mobile Edge Computing (MEC),

Innovations in edge-fog computing for emergency 
response
Beyond standard edge-fog architectures, recent inno­
vations in caching, latency mitigation, and predictive 
resource allocation have significantly improved health­
care network performance.
Proactive content caching for edge-fog healthcare networks
A key advancement in edge-fog computing is the use of 
proactive content caching, where frequently accessed 
medical data is stored closer to the edge, reducing 
retrieval times and enhancing real-time decision-mak­
ing. Patel et al. [25] reviewed proactive caching mecha­
nisms in edge computing, demonstrating improvements 
in cache hit probability, spectrum efficiency, and energy 
efficiency. Applying this caching strategy in edge-fog 
healthcare networks could optimize data availability dur­
ing emergency response situations.
Cold start latency mitigation in edge-fog architectures
Cold start latency remains a critical bottleneck in server­
less edge-fog computing environments, impacting real-
time healthcare applications. Golec et al. [26] conducted 
a systematic review of latency mitigation techniques, 
including checkpointing, predictive resource allocation, 
and application-based strategies. Their findings suggest 
that latency-aware function scheduling can significantly 
reduce response time in healthcare emergencies.
Predictive resource allocation using time-series forecasting
Optimising computational resource allocation in edge-
fog networks is crucial for ensuring system stability dur­
ing periods of high demand. Lee et al. [27] proposed 
Amazon Chronos-based time-series forecasting for pre­
dicting CPU utilization and dynamically allocating cloud 
resources. Integrating such proactive resource manage­
ment in edge-fog healthcare systems could enable bet­
ter workload distribution, preventing bottlenecks during 
large-scale emergencies.
AI-driven data caching for low-latency medical services
Wang and Friderikos [28] explored the application 
of Deep Learning (DL) for caching in edge networks, 
improving data retrieval efficiency and reducing cloud 
dependency. Their study emphasizes the importance of 
AI-driven caching mechanisms, particularly in environ­
ments where real-time access to patient data is critical.
Beyond foundational frameworks, several recent inno­
vations have been introduced to improve the scalability, 
scheduling accuracy, and low-latency behaviour of edge-
fog healthcare systems under unpredictable workloads.
Ghorbian et al. [29] conducted a comprehensive sur­
vey on scheduling in serverless computing, emphasizing 
that latency-aware scheduling is a pressing concern in 
fog-based emergency services. Their taxonomy highlights 
the importance of adaptive and event-driven scheduling 
models to avoid cold start delays—an area still underex­
plored in healthcare-specific edge-fog frameworks.
Amzil et al. [30] proposed a stochastic analysis of fog 
computing integrated with machine learning models to 
support scalable healthcare monitoring. While their sys­
tem demonstrated reduced average response time and 
energy consumption in large-scale simulations, it lacked 
a dynamic failover mechanism critical for emergency 
fault tolerance.
Choppara and Lokesh [31] applied DRL-based task 
scheduling for healthcare-focused fog systems, enhancing 
load balancing and resource utilization. However, their 
approach did not incorporate real-time edge-fog-cloud 
decision synchronization, leaving room for improvement 
in coordinated emergency response management.
These innovative studies collectively indicate a grow­
ing emphasis on intelligent task management. Still, the 
absence of an integrated model that combines predictive 
caching, DRL-based offloading, low-latency coordina­
tion, and secure data handling limits their effectiveness 
in real-world emergency care—gaps that the proposed 
Adaptive Edge-Fog Healthcare Network framework 
directly addresses.

Methodology
The proposed Adaptive Edge-Fog Healthcare Network 
framework aims to enhance emergency response man­
agement by leveraging the advantages of both edge and 
fog computing. This section of the framework explains 
the optimisation model, computational complexity, and 
practical, real-world applicability of the framework; for 
the benefit of readers who may not have a background 
in advanced optimisation theory, a broad description is 
provided, along with a flow chart that illustrates the main 
activities.
Problem formulation and objectives
However, the primary objective of the proposed frame­
work is to achieve improved latency and reduce energy 
consumption while processing healthcare data. This con­
cept proposes an edge fog cloud that combines the layers 
of edge, fog, and cloud. The edge layer is for processing, 
the fog layer is for storing actual data, and both layers 
act in real-time to meet the needs in emergency health­
care situations. More precisely, the methodology aims to 
reduce overall system latency while maximising the effi­
cient use of resources in edge and fog nodes.

analysis

the computational load according to dynamic require­
ments. We developed this allocation as an optimisa­
tion framework that aims to minimise node latency and 
energy utilisation, subject to meeting the computational 
limit at each node. The optimization model is designed to

Practical application scenario: emergency response case 
study
To illustrate the practical implementation of the pro­
posed edge-fog framework, we present an example 
based on an emergency healthcare response scenario in a 
densely populated area. Consider an urban hospital net­
work where real-time patient data, including heart rate 
and blood pressure, is continuously monitored via wear­
able IoT devices.
In the event of a sudden cardiac emergency, the follow­
ing processes are triggered:
1.	 Data collection at edge nodes: Wearable devices 
monitor vital signs, detecting anomalies such as 
irregular heart rates.
2.	 Local processing and alert generation: If the value 
exceeds a critical threshold, for instance, a heart rate 
of more than 120 bpm, the edge device triggers an 
alert to a nearby fog node.
3.	 Fog node allocation and analysis: Other devices in 
the vicinity of the patient are used to scrutinise the 
anomaly by the nearest fog node, with data collected 
from these devices in an aggregated form. If there is a 
positive result, then an emergency response message 
is dispatched in real-time to healthcare givers.
4.	 Resource optimisation and scalability adaptation: The 
dynamic resource allocation algorithm adjusts the 
distribution of computational loads among fog nodes 
to ensure low latency in response to increased alerts 
without overloading any specific fog node.
5.	 Secure data transmission to cloud: After the initial 
life-threatening situation has been treated, the 
patient’s data is shared, and only the non-identifying 
information remains in the cloud for analysis at a 
later time.
This scenario demonstrates that the proposed framework 
achieves low latency, facilitates efficient load distribu­
tion, and ensures high levels of system reliability during 
emergencies, which is crucial in dense healthcare net­
works in urban areas.
High-level overview of processes
To summarize, the methodology of the adaptive edge-fog 
healthcare framework consists of four core processes:
1.	 Data collection and local processing at edge nodes: 
Collect real-time healthcare data from IoT devices 
and perform initial anomaly detection.
2.	 Dynamic resource allocation across fog nodes: 
Optimize data flow by assigning edge nodes to fog 
nodes based on demand and resource availability.
3.	 Data aggregation and predictive analysis at fog 
nodes: Analyze incoming data at fog nodes and 
perform real-time predictive analytics.
4.	 Storage and long-term analysis at cloud layer: 
Transmit non-critical data to the cloud for historical 
analysis and machine learning model updates.

Dataset collection
In the case of the proposed Adaptive Edge-Fog Health­
care Network framework, patient-focused real-time 
medical data were sourced from multiple associated 
healthcare centres, primarily during emergency response 
operations. This dataset comprises cardiac rate, oxy­
gen levels, and blood pressure data collected from 
smartwatches and IoT health devices. Information was 
exchanged to the edge and fog nodes for processing of 
results obtained from the IoT devices. The collection 
period was 6 months and included more than 10,000 
emergency incidents. The patients’ information was de-
identified, and in accordance with information exchange 
security and privacy standards, the information exchange 
was secure. This dataset was used to evaluate the system’s 
performance under various loads, as well as in large-scale 
emergencies.
Dataset description
The data used in the Adaptive Edge-Fog Healthcare Net­
work framework is de-identified health data collected 
from various healthcare sources, including wearable 
devices and IoT Health Sensors. The dataset includes 
the patient’s heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, and 
oxygen saturation, measured at specified time intervals 
during emergencies. All entries are time-stamped and 
have associated metadata, including patient ID (pseud­
onymized), device type, and healthcare facility. There 
are almost 50,000 records from more than 5,000 patients 
across 12 healthcare centres. The data is structured into 
two categories: real-time monitoring data, which are 
essential for assessing the proposed system’s performance 
and efficiency under different network and emergency 
load scenarios. Below (Table 2) is the Dataset Description 
towards Adaptive Edge-Fog Healthcare Network.
The proposed Adaptive Edge-Fog Healthcare Net­
work was evaluated using real-world patient data col­
lected from Internet of Things (IoT)- enabled medical 
devices and electronic health records (EHRs). The data­
set includes vital signs such as heart rate, blood pressure, 
oxygen saturation, and temperature, along with histori­
cal patient records used for predictive analysis. Given the 
sensitive nature of healthcare data, strict anonymization 
and data privacy measures were implemented to ensure 
compliance with ethical and regulatory standards. To 
protect patient confidentiality, all personally identifiable 
information (PII) was removed before processing the 
data. A data anonymisation framework was implemented 
using hashing, encryption, and differential privacy tech­
niques to prevent unauthorised access.
Additionally, data was pseudonymized by replacing 
identifiers with random, unique codes, ensuring that 
patient records could not be traced back to individu­
als. Furthermore, all edge, fog, and cloud communica­
tion channels were secured using end-to-end encryption 
(AES-256 and TLS 1.3), preventing data breaches during 
transmission. The system also adheres to HIPAA (Health 
Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) and GDPR 
(General Data Protection Regulation) guidelines, ensur­
ing compliance with global healthcare data protection 
standards. By integrating anonymization techniques, 
encryption protocols, and strict access control mecha­
nisms, the proposed model ensures secure and pri­
vacy-preserving processing of patient health data while 
maintaining real-time emergency response capabilities.
The real-world dataset used in this study was collected 
from a smart hospital pilot program in Lahore, Pakistan, 
consisting of over 50,000 records of real-time patient 
vitals (heart rate, SpO₂, blood pressure) collected via 
edge-connected IoT wearables. All data was de-identified 
using SHA-256 pseudonymization of patient identifiers, 
and Gaussian noise injection was applied to ensure dif­

Proposed distributed Edge-Fog healthcare model
To accommodate healthcare data processing at the edge, 
fog, and cloud layers, the Distributed Edge-Fog Health­
care Model envisions a real-time, scalable, and fault-
tolerant response in emergencies. Edge computing is 
designed to perform initial analytics on the device. In 
contrast, fog computing handles intermediate analy­
sis through intermediate storage, and cloud comput­
ing is responsible for long-term storage and centralised 
optimisation. This part of the work describes in detail 
the structure of the model, along with the mathematical 
definition of the system, which includes how information 
flows, how resources are distributed, and how the system 
is optimised.
System model
The system is composed of three layers: edge, fog, and 
cloud. Each layer performs specific tasks to ensure that 
healthcare data is processed efficiently, decisions are 
made in real-time, and critical information is relayed to 
healthcare professionals as needed (see Fig. 2).
1.	 Edge layer: The edge layer consists of IoT-enabled 
devices (wearables, mobile apps, and health 
monitoring systems) that collect real-time patient 
data such as heart rate, body temperature, oxygen 
saturation, and glucose levels. These devices perform 
basic data processing to filter noise and detect 
anomalies.
2.	 Fog layer: The fog layer acts as an intermediary 
between the edge and the cloud. It is responsible 
for resource management, data aggregation, and 
predictive analytics, enabling more complex 
decisions to be made closer to the patient. The fog 
nodes can dynamically adjust their computational 
load in response to demand.
3.	 Cloud layer: The cloud layer manages long-term 
data storage, trains machine learning models, and 
facilitates global optimisation. It aggregates data from 
multiple fog nodes and uses advanced analytics for 
large-scale health system management.

Overhead analysis and time complexity of the proposed 
algorithm
Algorithm 1 describes the working logic of the proposed 
Latency-Aware Predictive Allocation with Cold Start 
Mitigation (LAPA-CSM), a core component of our adap­
tive edge-fog healthcare framework. The algorithm is 
designed to dynamically allocate patient data processing 
tasks to the most optimal computing node (edge or fog) 
in real time, minimizing latency and handling emergency 
load surges effectively.
It begins by initializing two key parameters:  σ threshold , 
the maximum acceptable jitter (i.e., fluctuation in delay), 
and  α  , the smoothing constant used for forecasting the 
future load on fog nodes. For each time interval  t , the 
algorithm first collects real-time vital sign data  V  from 
edge device  et  . It then uses exponential smoothing to 
predict the expected workload  Lt+1 , enabling preemp­
tive resource planning.
If the system detects that the standard deviation in 
delay exceeds the jitter threshold (i.e., the network is 
unstable or overloaded), it immediately reassigns the task 
to a backup fog node to avoid delay spikes. In cases where 
the selected fog node is found to be unavailable or already 
overloaded, the algorithm triggers a cold start mitigation 
process, which involves activating an idle fog node (cold 
node), pre-loading it with necessary runtime configura­
tions or lightweight models, and assigning the task to it.
Otherwise, if all systems are stable, the algorithm sim­
ply assigns the data processing task to the lowest-latency 
fog node with sufficient available CPU. If the incoming 
data indicates a critical health event—such as cardiac 
arrest or hypoxia—the algorithm simultaneously trig­
gers an emergency alert to notify medical staff. Finally, 
once the task is processed, the results and anonymized 
data are sent to the cloud for archival, analytics, or model 
retraining.
This algorithm ensures real-time responsiveness in 
healthcare environments by intelligently forecasting sys­
tem load, dynamically reallocating resources, mitigating 
cold start delays, and responding to emergency events 
with minimal latency.

The proposed Adaptive Edge-Fog Healthcare Network 
achieves efficient synchronisation among the edge, fog, 
and cloud layers through a structured and hierarchical 
communication mechanism. Each layer is designed to 
handle specific computational tasks, ensuring real-time 
processing, adaptive resource allocation, and seamless 
failover management in emergency healthcare scenarios. 
At the edge layer, IoT-enabled medical devices such as 
wearable health monitors, biosensors, and smart hospi­
tal equipment continuously collect real-time patient data. 
This data undergoes initial pre-processing at the edge, 
where basic anomaly detection algorithms filter non-crit­
ical information to reduce network congestion. In cases 
where immediate intervention is required (e.g., abnor­
mal heart rate detected), the processed data is pushed to 
the fog layer for further analysis and decision-making. 
The fog layer serves as the intermediate processing unit, 
receiving data from multiple edge nodes. It applies pre­
dictive AI models and machine learning-based health 
analytics to assess the severity of the condition. The fog 
layer manages dynamic resource allocation, ensuring that 
workloads are efficiently balanced across available fog 
nodes. In the event of a fog node failure, an automatic 
failover mechanism redirects tasks to backup fog nodes, 
ensuring system continuity and ensuring uninterrupted 
operation.
Additionally, the fog layer periodically synchronises 
with the cloud to upload non-urgent health data and 
retrieve AI-driven optimisations for improved real-time 
processing at the edge. The cloud layer serves as a cen­
tralised repository and a global optimisation hub. It 
stores historical patient records, conducts long-term 
AI training on healthcare trends, and refines predictive 
models that are periodically synchronized with the fog 
layer. The cloud also facilitates data backup and security 
monitoring, ensuring compliance with healthcare regu­
lations while safeguarding sensitive data. The synchro­
nisation between these layers is maintained through an 
event-driven messaging system, where edge devices trig­
ger priority-based data transmission based on the sever­
ity of the patient’s condition. High-priority alerts (e.g., a 
critical patient in an emergency) are immediately pro­
cessed at the fog layer.
In contrast, low-priority data (e.g., routine patient 
monitoring) is stored in the cloud for future analysis and 
review. Additionally, heartbeat signals and status updates 
ensure that each layer remains aware of the others’ avail­
ability, reducing system downtime and improving overall 
efficiency. By coordinating real-time data flow, intelli­
gent task allocation, and failover handling, the proposed 
edge-fog-cloud synchronization model guarantees high 
availability, low latency, and robust decision-making in 
emergency healthcare environments.

The proposed model is found to be superior to other

Conclusion
In this paper, the proposed new Edge-Fog Healthcare 
Network architecture aimed at enhancing emergency 
response management is described. They reduced latency 
due to hub and satellite integration, achieving 66.67% 
lower latency than classical systems Based on the cloud. 
Energy was also conserved with the Edge-Fog archi­
tecture having an energy efficiency of 92% compared to 
centrally based systems. Additionally, the presented sys­
tem’s performance has demonstrated a high tolerance to 
node failures, achieving a system reliability of 96%. How­
ever, some of these include the system’s inherent depen­
dence on the availability of edge and fog infrastructure, 
which can be a disadvantage in certain areas, as well as 
the costs associated with establishing fog nodes. In future 
research efforts, the system will be adapted to cope with 
the dynamic fluctuations of healthcare loads in real time 
and incrementally enhance data privacy through the use 
of encryption methods. Further studies will also be con­
ducted on the issue of using more sophisticated machine 
learning algorithms, even for predictive healthcare, to 
facilitate the early identification of strange health trends. 
Moreover, increasing the framework’s application capac­
ity for large-scale healthcare networks in several regions 
will be an essential goal. However, based on these cri­
tiques, the authors can assert that the Edge-Fog Health­
care Network responds to real emergencies by providing 
faster, more efficient, and more secure healthcare ser­
vices compared to a cloud-based model [36–39].

Abstract: The current healthcare system struggles to respond quickly enough to provide emergency medical care, particularly in remote or densely populated areas, or cannot scale to adequate levels of response in real-time. This paper presents an elaborate adaptive edge-fog healthcare network framework that supports Electronic Medical Records (EMR) through a multi-layer optimised solution. It also includes a real-time, decentralised processing model based on edge and fog computing architectures, which avoids the high latency typically required by most cloud- based systems when processing important data closer to its origin. To achieve this end, several novel features have been proposed within this framework, including a dynamic resource allocation algorithm that balances the computational load on the target edge and/or fog nodes as necessary to achieve optimal performance and prevent system failure. Furthermore, the operational environment of the framework incorporates robust and reliable methods for fault tolerance and data protection against leakage, even in low-connectivity networks or with node loss. Large-scale experiments demonstrate that the framework achieves a latency reduction rate of 66.67%, an energy consumption improvement of 92%, and a reliability of 96% in failure cases, thereby outcompeting cloud- only architectures in disaster recovery scenarios. Interestingly, the findings presented can demonstrate how the framework’s utilization may revolutionise healthcare emergency management by offering fast, safe, and efficient data-supported assistance in various care contexts.
